## Introduction
Working with large images can be painful in R. Whole slide images can exceedingly large (up to tens of Gigabytes). This
can easily saturate RAM memory. Indeed many popular image handling R packages (like EBImage or magick) have image size
limits that can be easily exceeded by whole slide images. 

CSM has inbuilt pipelines to deal with this situation. CSM implements functions to chop large images into manageable smaller crops. 
After image processing (either cell segmentation, cell phenotype labeling or image pixel thresholding), cell or image 
pixel information can be re-assembled to match the original whole slide coordinates.

In addition, CSM has in-built tools to downsize large images to more manageable smaller sized images. These downsized images can be used for
plotting purposes or to feed the `TMA_dearrayer_function()` (see below).


## Test datasets

The test datasets consists of two small 500x500 pixels breast carcinoma images. They have been stained with a multiplexed
immunofluorescence protocol for the following markers: "DAPI", "PDL1", "GZMB", "PD1", "CK-EPCAM", "CD8a", "FOXP3". 
The original images can be found at: https://immunoatlas.org/.

This is a trivial test dataset, as it contains very small images that could be easily handled by CSM. However, the principles
described in this example apply to larger whole-slide images.

```{r Images, eval = FALSE, results='hide'}
#Can only run in an interactive setting
#Generate a temporary directory to place the input images
Input_Dir <- tempfile(pattern = "tempdir1_Input")
dir.create(Input_Dir, recursive = TRUE)

#Save images in Input directory
purrr::map(1:2,
function(Image){
   EBImage::writeImage(CSM_MiniMultiTiff_test[[Image]],
   file.path(Input_Dir, names(CSM_MiniMultiTiff_test)[Image]))
})
```


## Check computing resources available
It is always a good idea to first check the CPU and RAM available.

```{r check, eval = TRUE}
Describe_my_computing_unit()
```

## Chopping large images
`Image_tile_deconstruction_function()` divides all the images in a directory into tiles. Accepted file extension include TIFF and OME.TIFF.
User can select the tile size (in pixels),the image channels to keep and the tile overlap. The smaller the tile size the easier it will 
be to work with the resulting chopped images, at the cost of an increased total tile number. If cell segmentation is going to be performed, 
tile overlap may be applied to account for segmentation artifacts due to edge proximity. Cell redundancy will be corrected in subsequent steps.
If RGB images need to be chopped, all RGB channels will be kept. The image chopping process is powered by the RBioFormats bioconductor R package. 

```{r chop, eval = FALSE}
#Can only run in an interactive setting
Input_Dir <- tempfile(pattern = "tempdir1_Input")
Output_Dir <- tempfile(pattern = "tempdir2_Output")
Mask_Dir <- tempfile(pattern = "tempdir3_masks")
Refined_Mask_Dir <- tempfile(pattern = "tempdir3_refined_masks")
dir.create(Input_Dir, recursive = TRUE)
dir.create(Output_Dir, recursive = TRUE)
dir.create(Mask_Dir, recursive = TRUE)
dir.create(Refined_Mask_Dir, recursive = TRUE)

#Save images in Input directory
purrr::map(1:2,
function(Image){
   EBImage::writeImage(CSM_MiniMultiTiff_test[[Image]],
   file.path(Input_Dir, names(CSM_MiniMultiTiff_test)[Image]))
})

#Perform tiling---------------------------------------------------
Image_tile_deconstruction_function(
   Directory = Input_Dir,
   Output_directory = Output_Dir,
   Ordered_Channels = c("DAPI", "PDL1", "GZMB", "PD1", "CK-EPCAM", "CD8a", "FOXP3"),
   Channels_to_keep = c("DAPI", "PDL1", "GZMB", "PD1", "CK-EPCAM", "CD8a", "FOXP3"),
   RGB_Color_images = FALSE,
   Tile_pixel_size = 250,
   Tile_Overlap = 50,
   N_cores = 1
)

#Check that files have been created-----------------------------------------
list.files(Output_Dir)
```

## Cell segmentation using tiled images
Cell segmentation and feature extraction proceeds as usual. First we need to generate the cellular segmentation masks.

```{r Segment, eval = FALSE}
#Can only run in an interactive setting
Watershed_cell_mask_generator(
    Directory = Output_Dir,
    Output_directory = Mask_Dir,
    Parameter_list = CSM_SegmentParams_test,
    N_cores = 1
)
```

After segmentation masks have been created, if there are overlaps between tiles (as in this case) there may be overlapping bias. In order to
account for this CSM implements two approaches. The first one (and most recommended) is to refine segmentation mask images using the
`Mask_conflict_resolver()`. This function analyzes overlapping areas between tiles and if there is any obvious conflict, it erodes pixels or whole cells
according to user defined priority scores. 

* __Distance to edge:__ The pixel or cell that is closest to the image edge will be removed. 
* __Cell size:__ The pixel or cell that belongs to the largest cell will remain.

A primary and a secondary priority score can be used if desired. The second approach (see below) is the use of the `Tile_to_image_cell_arrange_function()`
after cell feature matrix has been generated using the `Cell_feature_extractor()`.

```{r Refine, eval = FALSE}
Mask_conflict_resolver(
  Directory = Mask_Dir,
  Output_directory = Refined_Mask_Dir, 
  
  Resolution_approach = "Remove_whole_cells",
  Priority_type = c("Dist_to_edge", "Cell_size")
 )
```

After refined cell segmentation masks have been created cell features can be extracted using the `Cell_feature_extractor()` (see the Performing cell
segmentation vignette for more details about this function).
```{r Extract, eval = FALSE}
Cell_DATA_tiles <-
  Cell_feature_extractor(Image_directory = Output_Dir,
                         Mask_directory = Refined_Mask_Dir,
                         Ordered_Channels = CSM_SegmentParams_test[["Channels_to_keep"]],
                         Compute_basic_features = TRUE,
                         quantiles_to_calculate = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75),
                         Compute_texture_features = FALSE
                         )
```

After feature extraction has been performed, the resulting dataset needs to be formatted using the `Data_arrange_function()`. 
Then, original cell coordinates can be obtained by running `Tile_to_image_cell_arrange_function()`. If overlap correction has not been performed using the
`Mask_conflict_resolver()`, the overlap values can be corrected using the `Tile_to_image_cell_arrange_function()`. To this end the the `Tile_overlap` argument must be either
NULL or the overlap between tiles value. If NULL, the overlap value will be automatically computed. The cells that are closer to the edge than the `Dist_to_edge` argument
will be removed.

```{r Reassign_coordinates, eval = FALSE}
#Can only run in an interactive setting
#Arrange data
Cell_DATA_tiles <- 
  Data_arrange_function(
    DATA = Cell_DATA_tiles,
    X = 'm.cx',
    Y = "m.cy",
    Subject_Names = "image_id",
    Markers_to_keep = c("CK-EPCAM_mean", "CD8a_mean", "GZMB_mean")
)

#Return to original image X Y coordinates
Cell_DATA_WholeImage <-
  Tile_to_image_cell_arrange_function(
    DATA = Cell_DATA_tiles
)

#Check that results are OK
Cell_DATA_WholeImage %>% 
  dplyr::filter(Subject_Names == "ABCM22001_B09_MiniCrop.tiff") %>%
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(x = X, y = Y)) + ggplot2::geom_point()

```

All these functions that are based on tiles work identifying patterns in the the file name. These files do not contain any relevant metadata.
Therefore, manipulation of the file name can result in unexpected results. __PLEASE AVOID FILE NAME MODIFICATIONS!__

## Pixel thresholding of tiled images and re-assembled images
Single channels can be pixel-thresholded using image chunks. Afterwards thresholded image chunks can be used to re-assemble a 
thresholded whole image using the `Image_from_tile_rebuilder()` function. Since image chunks will be used in the thresholding process,
LOCAL thresholding using automatic algorithms can be extremely problematic (high risk of setting thresholds according to local artifacts).
Therefore, GLOBAL thresholding is highly recommended.

If images are being chopped to be thresholded, overlap between images is not supported. Although no error will be thrown by the 
related functions, the re-build process of overlapping tiles will result in aberrant re-assembled images.
```{r Tile_threshold, eval = FALSE}
#Can only run in an interactive setting
Input_Dir <- tempfile(pattern = "tempdir1_Input")
Output_Dir_tiles <- tempfile(pattern = "tempdir2_Output")
Output_Dir_tiles_thresholded <- tempfile(pattern = "tempdir3_Output")
Output_Dir_reconstruction <- tempfile(pattern = "tempdir4_Output")
dir.create(Input_Dir, recursive = TRUE)
dir.create(Output_Dir_tiles, recursive = TRUE)
dir.create(Output_Dir_tiles_thresholded, recursive = TRUE)
dir.create(Output_Dir_reconstruction, recursive = TRUE)

#Save images in Input directory
purrr::map(1:2,
function(Image){
   EBImage::writeImage(CSM_MiniMultiTiff_test[[Image]],
   file.path(Input_Dir, names(CSM_MiniMultiTiff_test)[Image]))
})

#Divide images into tiles------------------------------------------------------
Image_tile_deconstruction_function(
   Directory = Input_Dir,
   Output_directory = Output_Dir_tiles,
   Ordered_Channels = c("DAPI", "PDL1", "GZMB", "PD1", "CK-EPCAM", "CD8a", "FOXP3"),
   Channels_to_keep = c("DAPI", "PDL1", "GZMB", "PD1", "CK-EPCAM", "CD8a", "FOXP3"),
   RGB_Color_images = FALSE,
   Tile_pixel_size = 250,
   Tile_Overlap = 0,
   N_cores = 1
)

#Threshold the CK_EPCAM channel of tiles
Pixel_Threshold_calculator(
     N_cores = 1,
     Directory = Output_Dir_tiles,
     Ordered_Channels = c("DAPI", "PDL1", "GZMB", "PD1", "CK-EPCAM", "CD8a", "FOXP3"),
     Channels_to_keep = c("DAPI", "PDL1", "GZMB", "PD1", "CK-EPCAM", "CD8a", "FOXP3"),
     Target_channel = "CK-EPCAM",

     Save_processed_images = TRUE,
     Output_Directory = Output_Dir_tiles_thresholded,

     Local_thresholding = FALSE,
     Threshold_type = "Arbitrary",
     Threshold_value = 0.02,

     Threshold_type_tissueMask = "Absolute",
     Threshold_value_tissueMask = 0.001,
     Blurr_tissueMask = TRUE,
     Sigma_tissueMask = 0.5,
     Blurr_target = FALSE
)

#Rebuild images from tiles-----------------------
Image_from_tile_rebuilder(
   Directory = Output_Dir_tiles_thresholded,
   Output_directory = Output_Dir_reconstruction,
   RGB_Color_images = FALSE,
   N_cores = 1
)

#Check the files created-------------------------------------------------
list.files(Output_Dir_reconstruction)

#Remove directories---------------------------------------------------------
unlink(c(Input_Dir, Output_Dir_tiles, Output_Dir_tiles_thresholded, Output_Dir_reconstruction), recursive = TRUE)
```

## Downsizing large images
The CSM function `Smart_image_importer()` is capable of importing to the R session a downsized version of very large images.
The user must first provide the path to the image and the desired maximum number of pixels (in log10 scale) that the output
image will have (1 million max pixels by default).

In addition, the user can subset the image by cropping it or select specific image channels to be kept. The output image can be saved by
setting the `Save_processed_images = TRUE`.

How does the `Smart_image_importer()` work? First, the function will obtain image metadata (file type, pixel size, number of channels...).
If the image is smaller than 1.5Gb in size, it will attempt importing the image directly followed by downsizing. If the image is larger
than 1.5Gb it will sequentially import image chunks(tiles) and downsized them. Afterwards it will merge the chunks(tiles) back into a single
image. The function is designed to generate tiles that are around 0.5Gb in size.

```{r Smart_importer, eval = TRUE, fig.align='center', out.width='100%', fig.width = 10, fig.height = 8}
#Create temporary input directory------------------------------
Input_Dir <- tempfile(pattern = "tempdir1_Input")
dir.create(Input_Dir, recursive = TRUE)

#Save images in Input directory
purrr::map(1:2,
function(Image){
   EBImage::writeImage(CSM_MiniMultiTiff_test[[Image]],
   file.path(Input_Dir, names(CSM_MiniMultiTiff_test)[Image]))
})

#reduce the pixel content of the image
Image <- Smart_image_importer(Image_directory = dir(Input_Dir, full.names = TRUE)[1], 
                     Log10_pixel_output = 5
)

print(Image)
```

Downsized images can be subsequently used for plotting purposes (for example using the `Image_channel_color_merger()` to combine several
channels into a single RGB color image). In addition, the `Smart_image_importer()` is also the function used by several Shiny APPs
implemented in CSM to import large images.

## De-arraying TMAs
Tissue micro-arrays (TMAs) are usually large whole slide images that require individual core image extraction before proceeding with 
analyses. The `TMA_dearrayer_function()` serves this purpose. It requires a downsized version of the whole slide TMA image. The function will use 
this downsized image to identify where tissue cores are located.

* __Tissue mask generation:__ First, the image is thresholded to find foreground (tissue) and background pixels. Foreground pixels will be used in
subsequent processing. To this end, the user may choose different strategies (identical to the approaches for tissue mask generation implemented
in `Pixel_Threshold_calculator()`). In our experience, it is best to use the arbitrary method and try various cut-off values to select the most
appropriate. 

* __Tissue mask processing:__ After obtaining the binary (foreground/background) pixel mask, the image will be processed to fill wholes. Then, erosion
followed by dilation can be applied according to user preferences. These pre-processing steps polish the initial mask and ease out the subsequent
watershed algorithm that will be applied to identify individual core areas. The choices of erosion and dilation round number and kernel size will be 
guided by the amount of noise in the image, the presence of tissue detachment or crush artifact and the size of the cores.

* __Tissue mask watersheding:__ The processed tissue mask is the subjected to a watershed algorithm to identify individual tissue core areas. To this end
the mask is first transformed to a distance map were the value of foreground pixels is equal to the distance of every pixel to the closest background
pixel. This allows the watershed algorithm to separate cores even when there are touching edges (that may occur in heavily populated TMAs). Two 
parameters influence the results of watershed algorithms in the case there are touching TMA cores: tolerance and extension (corresponding to
the `Watershed_tolerance` and `Watershed_ext` function arguments). High tolerance values will 
result in merging of TMA cores. The same is true for the extension parameter. Keeping the tolerance low (below 1) and low extension values (below 10) 
maximize the number of cores identify, at the cost of sometimes splitting a single tissue core into several pieces. At the end of this process the
function will return the identified cores and the user will have the opportunity to stop the function and refine parameters if required.

* __Estimate the number of rows and columns:__ The function will then compute the X and Y centroid coordinates for every core and will determine the 
number of rows and columns present in the TMA and the row and column index where every core belongs. This process is relevant as it will be used to label
each core after extraction, and if the user provides a matrix of core names, the row/col information will be used to match cores and names provided.
To this end, the function will use hierarchical clustering to group the core coordinates. This process can be refined modifying the `Tolerance_column`
and `Tolerance_row` arguments. Small tolerance values require striking distances between individual rows and columns to be identified. After performing
this step, the function will return the bounding box and provisional labels of the identified cores and the user may have the opportunity to stop the 
function and refine parameters if required.

* __Add user provided core labels:__ This is an optional by __HIGHLY ENCOURAGED__ step. User can provide a matrix or a dataframe/tibble containing 
core labels. The function will take this information, match the matrix according to the number of rows/columns of the matrix and the identified cores, 
and proceed to label the cores according to user preferences. Importantly, the matrix must not contain duplicated names. Cores that are known by the 
user to be empty should be indicated using NA_value. After performing labelling, the function will return the results of the alignment. The user can then
switch rows or column order or transverse the provided matrix at will until the labels match exactly with the tissue cores.

* __Extract tissue core images:__ Finally, the function will compute the bounding box of the cores in the original image. Individual TMA cores will
be subsetted from the original image using the `Smart_image_importer()`. Each image will be saved in the desired output directory.

```{r TMA_dearray, eval = FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='100%', fig.width = 10, fig.height = 8}
TMA_image_downsized <-
    Smart_image_importer(Image_directory = "Path/to/original/TMA/Image", 
                         Log10_pixel_output = 6
  ) 
  
TMA_dearrayer_function(Original_Image_Directory = "Path/to/original/TMA/Image", 
                      Downsized_Image = TMA_image_downsized, 
                      Output_Directory = "Path/to/ouput/directory")

```

## Merging channels
Multiple channels can be merged into a single RGB colored images using CSM. This can be achieved by the `Image_channel_color_merger` function. In order to run the function the user
must have imported a `magick` object generated using the `magick::image_read()` function or the `Smart_image_importer` function. In addition, the user must prepare a list containing
the parameters used to merge the channels. Each item of the list must be named. List items are also lists containing the following items:

* __channel_index:__ A numeric value indicating the channel position to be merged.

* __color:__ A character value (either color name or HEX value) indicating the color to be used to for the designated channel.

* __gamma:__ A numeric value between a between 0.001 and 1000 indicating the gamma correction.

* __min:__ A numeric value higher than 0 and lower than 1 (and lower than max) to adjust white level.

* __max:__ A numeric value higher than 0 and lower than 1 (and higher than min) to adjust white level.

* __equalize:__ A logical value indicating if equaliztion should be performed on the designated channel.

The image channel color merger powers the channel merging capabilities of shiny apps deployed in CSM.

```{r Color_merging, eval = TRUE, fig.align='center', out.width='100%', fig.width = 10, fig.height = 8}
#Get the image
Image <- magick::image_read(CSM_MiniMultiTiff_test[[2]])

#Generate the merging parameters (in this case 4 channels will be merged)----
Merge_parameter_list <- 
  list(
      DAPI = list(channel_index = 1,
                  color = "blue",
                  gamma = 1,
                  min = 0,
                  max = 80,
                  equalize = FALSE),

      CK = list(channel_index = 5,
                color = "white",
                gamma = 1.1,
                min = 5,
                max = 20,
                equalize = FALSE),
 
      CD8 = list(channel_index = 6,
                 color = "#f0703a",
                 gamma = 1,
                 min = 10,
                 max = 30,
                 equalize = FALSE),

      GZMB = list(channel_index = 3,
                  color = "cyan",
                  gamma = 1,
                  min = 5,
                  max = 20,
                  equalize = FALSE)

)

#Perform the merging
Image_channel_color_merger(Image = Image,
                          Parameter_list = Merge_parameter_list)

```

## Multiple dataset alignment
Certain experiments require multiple serial sections of the same tissue sample. The most obvious example is the use of serial sections to perform 3D analysis of tissue architecture.
For example, certain projects may involve performing several multiplexed immunofluorescence panels performed on serial tissue sections. 
Each multiplex immunfluoresence panel evaluates up to 7-10 different proteins. In order to combine the information obtained from the individual sections, spatial
alignment needs to be carried out. Using CSM, the user can perform spatial alignment based on cell spatial coordinates information using the `Cell_aligner_function`.

The `Cell_aligner_function` assumes that there is a spatial coherence between the samples provided. The function performance will increase as the similarity between spatial distribution
patterns is more patent. Given two cell spatial distributions, the function will consider one of them as the reference (immovable) and the other as movable (moving points). 
In order to reduce the spatial noise present in cell spatial distribution coordinates the user can take one or more of the following approaches:

* __Work with specific cell phenotypes:__ In stead of working with all cell datapoints, the user can select those points belonging to certain cell types. For example, tumor cells show a trend to 
display tissue-specific spatial clustering distributions. These distributions can be more spatially robust and consistent between slides than using whole cell spatial patterns.

* __Apply DBSCAN filtering:__ By removing cells that are not spatially clustered, spatial patterns can be made more evident. 

* __Work on the spatial concave hull:__ In stead of working on cell spatial coordinates, the concave hull of the cell outline can be computed. The overall shape of the cell distribution will be used
to align different slides.

This is how the  `Cell_aligner_function` works:

* __1<sup>st</sup> Perform pre-processing:__ Apply cell phenotype and/or DBSCAN filtering and compute concave hull if required.

* __2<sup>nd</sup> Align X and Y centroids of cell spatial coordinates:__ The spatial coordinates of the moving points are translated to match the centroid of the reference points.

* __3<sup>rd</sup> Perform initial ICP:__ The Iterative Closest Point (ICP) is applied (based on the `Morpho::icpmat`). The ICP is an heuristic algorithm that translates and rotates points to 
minimize the distance between each point in the moving dataset and it's closest neighbor in the reference dataset. The error of the model (average min distance from all points to their closest neighbor 
in their homologous dataset) is recorded.

* __4<sup>th</sup> Perform final ICP after rotation and flipping:__ The ICP algorithm results are greatly influenced by the initial distribution of the moving point pattern. In order to reduce the chances
of finding local minima, the ICP is repeated after rotating and flipping the moving dataset before application (none, X and Y flipping and 360 degrees rotation tried. 1,080 combinations are always tried).
The error of the model is recorded. The model with the lowest error is retained.

* __5<sup>th</sup> Apply the model to all the datapoints if needed:__ When the alignment has been computed using a subset of the points (any sort of pre-processing has been performed) the model needs to be 
applied to the whole moving point dataset. 

* __6<sup>th</sup> Apply a final ICP step using the whole dataset:__ Sometimes, a final ICP performed on all the cells once the model has been applied can help to improve minor errors in the 
alignment process. Other times this step is counterproductive. 

When a single tissue has been sliced several times, the function can handle multi-slide alignment at once. To this end the function will use the first slide as absolute reference. In a multi-step process
the other non-reference cell spatial distributions will be aligned to the reference slide. First the second slide will be aligned to the absolute reference. Afterwards the thirds slide is process to be
aligned with the already aligned version of the second slide and so on. Although it would be much simpler to align all tissue slides to the absolute reference, we assume that there is higher
spatial coherence between consecutive slides. It is reasonable to believe that doing the alignment in this way will improve the overall results.

To demonstrate the way the aligner works we will first generate a reference dataset (the CSM_Phenotypecell_test). We will generate a rotated version of the reference dataset where each sample
will be randomly rotated between 15 and 345 degrees. We will also generate a dataset that will be randomly X or Y flipped and translated by a random number of pixels. Finally, these
datasets will be placed in a list that will be fed to the `Cell_aligner_function`.

```{r Random_dataet, eval = FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='100%', fig.width = 10, fig.height = 8}
#Get the original dataset
Original_dataset <- CSM::CSM_Phenotypecell_test

#Generate a randomly rotated version
Rotated_dataset <-
  purrr::map_dfr(unique(Original_dataset$Subject_Names), function(Subject) {
    #obtain each individual sample
    Individual_sample <- Original_dataset %>% dplyr::filter(Subject_Names == Subject)
    #Compute a random degree
    Random_degrees <- sample(15:345, size = 1)
    Random_radians <- Random_degrees * pi / 180
    
    Individual_sample[c("X", "Y")] <- Rotate_points(as.matrix(Individual_sample[c("X", "Y")]),
                                                    theta = Random_radians,
                                                    non_negative = TRUE)
    
    return(Individual_sample)
  })
#Generate a randomly flipped and translated
Flipped_Translated_dataset <-
  purrr::map_dfr(unique(Original_dataset$Subject_Names), function(Subject) {
    #obtain each individual sample
    Individual_sample <- Original_dataset %>% dplyr::filter(Subject_Names == Subject)
    #Compute a random flipping
    Random_flipping <- sample(c("x", "y"), size = 1)
    Individual_sample[c("X", "Y")] <- Flip_xy(as.matrix(Individual_sample[c("X", "Y")]), mode = Random_flipping)
    
    #Compute a random translation
    Random_X_translation <- sample(seq(from = 25, to = 100, by = 25), size = 1)
    Random_Y_translation <- sample(seq(from = 25, to = 100, by = 25), size = 1)
    Individual_sample$X <- Individual_sample$X + Random_X_translation
    Individual_sample$Y <- Individual_sample$Y + Random_Y_translation
    
    return(Individual_sample)
  })

#Place them inside a list
DATASETS_LIST <-
  list(
    Reference = Original_dataset,
    Rotated = Rotated_dataset,
    Flipped_translated = Flipped_Translated_dataset
  )
```

Next we will execute the `Cell_aligner_function` function. We will use the whole cell dataset but computing the concave hull to work with tissue outlines in stead of the bare cell spatial coordinates.
Afterwards we will plot the result to confirm that the algorithm has performed adequately.

```{r Align, eval = FALSE, fig.align='center', out.width='100%', fig.width = 10, fig.height = 8}
Aligned <-
  Cell_aligner_function(
    N_cores = 1,
    Cell_feature_list = DATASETS_LIST,
    Iterations = 5,
    Phenotypes_included = NULL,
    
    Apply_DBSCAN_denoise = FALSE,
    
    Concave_Hull = TRUE,
    Hull_ratio = 0.1,
    Polygon_sampling_density = 5,
    
    Perform_final_ICP_refinement = FALSE
  )



#Plot the results
plot(
  purrr::map_dfr(1:length(Aligned$Cell_feature_list), function(List_item) {
    Item <- Aligned$Cell_feature_list[[List_item]] %>% dplyr::mutate(Modification = names(Aligned$Cell_feature_list)[List_item])
  }) %>%
    ggplot(aes(X, Y, color = Modification)) +
    facet_wrap( ~ Subject_Names) +
    geom_point(size = 3)
)
```

In order to achieve the desired results, multiple approaches are usually required. Do not despair.


```{r Session_info, eval = TRUE, fig.align='center', out.width='100%', fig.width = 10, fig.height = 8}
sessionInfo()
```
